        "content": "IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON SIGNAL PROCESSING, VOL., NO., 1 Wide-Band Cyclic Cross-Correlation Processing Antonio Napolitano, Fellow, IEEE Abstract—The wide-band cyclic cross-correlation function (WB-CCCF) is introduced for finite average-power signals. It is the cyclic cross-correlation of a signal and a time-scaled version of another signal. Input-output relationships in terms of WBCCCFs are derived for the wide-band Doppler channel, that is, the channel that introduces a complex gain, a delay, a frequency shift, and a time-scale factor on the complex envelope of the input signal. These relationships are exploited to design new algorithms for estimating time-difference-of-arrival, frequency-differenceof-arrival, and time-scale ratio of the signals impinging on a pair of sensors when the transmitter is a high-speed—possibly hypersonic—source emitting a wide-band radio-frequency signal. In the presence of severe noise and interference environments, the proposed algorithms exhibit the typical signal-selectivity property of cyclostationarity-based estimation techniques. Moreover, unlike existing methods, they provide satisfactory performance when the so called narrow-band condition is not satisfied, that is when the product of signal bandwidth and length of the observation interval is not much smaller than the ratio of medium propagation speed and source radial speed. The new techniques are exploited for the problem of locating a very low Earth orbit satellite and a hypersonic re-entry vehicle. Index Terms—cyclostationarity, wide-band ambiguity function, moving source localization, Doppler, hypersonic vehicle. I. INTRODUCTION The problem of passive detection and range and velocity estimation of a moving radio-frequency source is encountered in several applications including navigation and surveillance. Measurements of the time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) and the frequency-difference-of-arrival (FDOA) of the wavefront impinging on several pairs of spatially separated sensors allows one to locate the source and to estimate its velocity [8], [28], [34]. Classical approaches assume that, for each sensor, the so called narrow-band condition is satisfied. That is, the product of the transmitted signal bandwidth and the length of the observation interval is much smaller than the ratio of the medium propagation speed and the relative radial speed between source and receiver. In such a case, the Doppler effect is modeled as a frequency shift of the carrier and does not influence the complex envelope of the received signal [19, Sec. 7.5], [37, Sec. 9.1]. In additive Gaussian noise, the estimation procedure leads to consider the the narrow-band cross-ambiguity function (NB-CAF)—a function of frequency shift and delay—of the received signals on each pair of sensors [11], [37, Chap. 10]. In the presence of high relative radial speeds and/or wideband sources, the narrow-band condition is not satisfied even for moderately large observation intervals and a time-scale or time-stretch-or-compression factor in the argument of the A. Napolitano is with Universit`a di Napoli “Parthenope”, Department of Engineering, Napoli, Italy (email: antonio.napolitano@uniparthenope.it). complex envelope of the received signal must be accounted for. Such a model is appropriate in processing signals in global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) [26], [30] or signals transmitted by spatial probes [25]. In such a case, the wide-band cross-ambiguity function (WB-CAF)—a function of time-scale factor and delay—is adopted for detection and estimation of TDOA and time-scale ratio (TSR) [15], [32], [39]. In very challenging scenarios, strong nonstationary possibly intentional interference signals contaminate the useful signals on the sensors and the approaches based on the NB-CAF and WB-CAF perform poorly. In order to get better performance, the signal-selectivity property of cyclostationaritybased algorithms [7, Chap. 14], [21, Chaps. 8, 9] has been successfully exploited to design interference-tolerant TDOA estimation methods [2], [8], [9], and joint FDOA and TDOA estimation methods [12], [13]. In all these cyclostationaritybased techniques, the narrow-band condition is assumed to be valid in modeling the received signals. In this paper, the wide-band cyclic cross-correlation function (WB-CCCF) is introduced. It is the cyclic crosscorrelation of a signal and a time-scaled version of another signal. It is a function of cycle frequency, time-scale factor, and delay. New input/output relationships in terms of WBCCCFs are derived for the wide-band Doppler channel, that is, the channel that introduces a complex gain, a delay, a frequency shift, and a time-scale factor on the complex envelope of the input signal. Starting from these relationships, new estimators for TSR, FDOA, and TDOA, based on WBCCCF measurements on two sensors are derived when an almost-cyclostationary (ACS) signal is transmitted by a highspeed moving source. The results are relevant since almost all signals adopted in communications, radar/sonar, and telemetry are ACS [7, Chap. 12], [21, Chap. 7]. The new estimators have the same signal-selectivity property of cyclostationarity-based estimators. Moreover, unlike previously proposed techniques, they do not require that the narrow-band condition be satisfied. Thus, they exhibit satisfactory performance in scenarios with wider bandwidths, higher speeds, and larger observation intervals with respect to those allowed for methods that assume the narrow-band condition be satisfied. The estimators are shown to exhibit satisfactory performance in the case of hypersonic vehicles when classical estimators fail due to the non validity of the narrow-band condition. The (conjugate) wide-band cyclic cross-correlation function is defined as χα yx(∗) (σ, τ ) ≜ D y(t) x(∗)(σ(t − τ )) e−j2παtE t. A slightly different definition of WB-CCCF is considered in [22], where the complex exponential is e−j2πσαt. Functions similar to the WB-CCCF (4.1) with (∗) = ∗ are considered in [30] in the context of GNSS and in [38] for bistatic radars. In contrast, the WB-CCCF (4.1) is defined for finite-power signals in terms of an infinite time average. Furthermore, the frequency shift ν and the time-scale-factor σ in the functions in [30] and [38] are both related to the Doppler effect and are linked by the relationship ν = (σ − 1)fc, where fc is the transmitted signal carrier frequency (see (2.5)). In contrast, in the WB-CCCF, frequency shift α and time-scale σ are independent parameters. As explained in Section VI, the frequency shift in the WBCCCF is related to a cycle frequency of the ACS signal x(t). Discussion Equations (9.7) and (9.9) reveal that estimation methods based on the WB-CCCF have the same signal selectivity property that is characteristic of classical cyclostationaritybased estimation algorithms. Specifically, these estimation methods are intrinsically immune to the effects of noise and interference, regardless of the possible temporal and spectral overlap of SOI and disturbance signals, at arbitrarily low levels of SNR and signal-to-interference ratio (SIR), provided that mild assumptions (AS2, AS3) on the cyclostationarity properties of SOI and disturbances are fulfilled. Thus, these estimation methods are highly tolerant to noise and interference in practice, provided that a sufficiently large observation interval is adopted for WB-CCCF measurements, the performance being limited only by the cycle leakage effect [7, Chap. 13], [21, Secs. 5.3.4, 9.7], that is, the leakage of SOI’s and disturbances’ cycle frequencies different from α0 on the cyclic feature measurements at cycle frequency α0. The lower the SNR and SIR, the larger the required data-record length. It is worthwhile to underline that the asymptotic noise immunity of classical cyclostationarity-based algorithms holds provided that the observed signals can be modeled as singularly and jointly ACS. That is, provided that the narrowband condition (2.6) is satisfied (si = 1 in the argument of the complex envelope in (2.3)). Consequently, these classical algorithms have an upper bound for the maximum allowed data-record length and, hence, a lower bound for the minimum SNR and SIR for which satisfactory performance can be achieved. In contrast, estimation algorithms based on the WB CCCF exploit a higher fidelity description of the Doppler effect, (si ̸= 1 in the argument of the complex envelope in (2.3)) and do not have the upper bound on the datarecord length imposed by (2.6). Hence, they are effective with data-record lengths much larger than those allowed for the classical cyclostationarity-based methods and are expected to provide good performance at lower values of SNR and SIR with respect to those for which classical cyclostaionarity-based methods are effective. Such a better performance behavior is confirmed by the numerical experiments in Section XIII. X. With respect to WB-SPECCOA, the WB-CCCF-based methods have a significantly larger TDOA operating range. In fact, for the WB-CCCF-based methods, the maximum absolute value of the TDOA that can be estimated is only limited by the data-record length T. Thus, the observed signals r1,T (t) and r(∗) 2,T (σ(t − τ )) in (7.1) (with y ≡ r2 and x ≡ r1) could not significantly overlap or could not overlap at all. In such a case, r1,T (t) and r2,T (t) must be collected by using the same time reference (e.g., by using a GPS time reference) and then time shifted by known quantities in order to have a substantial time overlap of the two signals before computing the estimate (7.1) (and the estimates of cyclic cross-statistics, NB-CAF, and WB-CAF). These known time shifts are then accounted for in the final computation of τ△. In addition, note that, for the estimation of cross statistics, the samples of the two signals r1,T (t) and r2,T (t) and the corresponding time references should be made available at a fusion center (possibly coincident with the locus of one of the two sensors) through a service channel. The delay introduced by this channel depends on the distance between sensor(s) and fusion center, is known, and must be accounted for in the final computation of τ△. In model (2.2), the disturbances ni(t) also account for the noise on this service channel. XII. COMPUTATIONAL COMPLEXITY Let be T = N Ts, where Ts is the sampling period and N the number of samples of the received signals. A. (Conjugate) Cycle Frequency Estimation The computational complexity of the cycle frequency estimation (Table III) is due to the computation of the discretetime implementation of the cyclic correlogram (3.7) in (9.11) for several values of the lag parameter and to the maximum search procedure. For each value of the lag parameter, the discrete-time cyclic correlogram is computed by the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) in the frequency interval α ∈ [αmin, αmax]. This is efficiently done by the CZT whose computational complexity is O(N log2 N ) [27]. The number of lags is nτ = ⌊T /Ts⌋, where T is the (approximate) width of the cyclic autocorrelation of ri(t). Thus, nτ does not depend on N. The search of the maximum over N values of α has computational complexity O(N ). For conjugate cycle frequencies we obtain the same result. Therefore, the overall computational complexity of the (conjugate) cycle frequency estimation is O(N log2 N ). B. Method I The computational complexity of Method I (Table IV) is due to the computation of the function (9.14), that is, of the wide-band cyclic cross-correlogram (7.1) for fixed values of cycle frequency ad scale parameter. It requires a time-scale changing with fixed time-scale factor implemented by CZT with complexity O(N log2 N ) and a correlation implemented via FFT with complexity O(N log2 N ). Let nτ be the number of lags to be considered. It depends on the minimum and maximum range that must be monitored and does not depend on N. Thus the mono-dimensional search over nτ lag points in (9.15) has complexity not depending on N. Therefore, the overall complexity of Method I is O(N log2 N ). C. Method II The computational complexity of Method II (Table V) is due to the computation of the wide-band cyclic cross-correlogram (7.1) as a function of the two variables σ and τ for a fixed value of γb1 and to the bi-dimensional search procedure. For each fixed value of σ, the computational complexity of the wide-band cyclic cross-correlogram is O(N log2 N ) as for Method I. Let ∆σ = 1/(BT ) be the scale resolution, where B is the bandwidth of the complex envelope. If ∆smax is the maximum scale deviation from 1 (see (9.2)), the number of points on the scale axis is nσ = ⌈2∆smax/∆σ⌉ = ⌈2∆smaxBN Ts⌉. Thus, the complexity of the estimation of nσ values of the wide-band cyclic cross-correlogram (7.1) is O(N 2 log2 N ). The number of lags nτ to be considered in (9.17) does not depend on N as for Method I. Therefore, the search of the maximum over nσnτ points has complexity O(nσnτ ) = O(N ). Therefore, the overall complexity of Method II is O(N 2 log2 N ). The higher computational complexity of Method II with respect to Method I is compensated by a better TDOA estimation performance (Figs. 9 (left) and 12 (left)). It is the cyclic cross-correlation of a signal and a timescaled version of another signal. For the wide-band Doppler channel, input/output relations in terms of WB-CCCFs are derived for both analytic signals and complex envelopes. Moreover, the special case of input almost-cyclostationary signal is considered. New estimators are proposed for estimating the TSR, FDOA, TDOA, and CGR of the noisy signals received by a pair of sensors when a high-speed moving source emits a wide-band radio-frequency signal. By considering the estimates obtained by more sensor pairs, the source can be localized and its velocity estimated. The WB-CCCF possesses the typical signal selectivity properties of classical cyclic statistical functions. From the knowledge of the range in which the transmitted cycle frequency can fall, for each sensor the received cycle frequency, as modified by the wide-band Doppler channel, is estimated and is adopted as cycle frequency in the WB-CCCF. Thus, under very mild assumptions on the noise terms, the proposed estimation algorithms are shown to be highly tolerant to noise and interference, provided that a sufficiently large observation interval is adopted for the WB-CCCF estimates. An admissible source region is identified in the scale/cycle-frequency plane where scale factors and cycle frequencies of the emitting source can lie. It is not assumed that the so called narrow-band condition is verified. That is, it is not assumed that the product of signal bandwidth and length of the observation interval is much smaller than the ratio of the medium propagation speed and the relative radial speed between transmitter and receiver. Therefore, the proposed estimation algorithms provide satisfactory performance in the presence of larger observation intervals, larger bandwidths, and higher velocities (e.g., hypersonic) of the source with respect to those allowed for the classical algorithms that require the narrow-band condition be satisfied. It is observed that for (narrow-band) cyclostationarity-based algorithms, the asymptotic performance cannot be reached by augmenting without bound the length of the observation interval since the constraint imposed by the narrow-band condition must be satisfied. In contrast, the estimation methods based on the WB-CCCF relax such an assumption and can operate with larger observation intervals, and hence, they are more efficient to counteract the effects of noise and interference. Numerical experiments for the problem of locating a VLEO satellite and a re-entry vehicle are conducted in the presence of strong disturbance signals on the two sensors, including jammer signals impinging (with different delays) on both sensors. Increasing the observation interval in order to counteract the effects of interference improves the performance of the WB-CCCF based estimation methods. In contrast, competitive cyclostationarity-based methods improve performance when the data record starts to increase but perform poorly when the data-record length is such that the narrow-band condition is not satisfied.
